prompt.context: Our client is Avicenna Health, a major healthcare payer in the Chicagoland area. Avicenna Health recently purchased a large hospital system in order to compete with a former strategic partner, University Medical Center (UMC), one of the best hospital systems in the nation. The client believes that as a provider and payer, it will be better positioned for the future of healthcare which will focus on value of care, rather than volume. Nonetheless, our client is concerned about the profitability of its hospitals today and in the future, since the majority of patients are choosing UMC.
prompt.question: What should the client do to position itself more successfully in the short and long-term?

clarifying_info.a: A payer is a healthcare insurance company.
A provider is a hospital or healthcare setting.
Value refers to reimbursement based on quality and appropriateness of care, as opposed to volume which is reimbursement based on quantity of care.

exhibits.title: Suggested Framework (Interviewer Guide)
exhibits.shows: Interviewer guide page showing the suggested framework structure and criteria for evaluating candidate responses (good vs. better candidate descriptions).

exhibits.title: Table of Non-Hospital Sites of Care
exhibits.shows: A table comparing four non-hospital sites of care across multiple dimensions: target demographic, relative utilization, hospital replacement rate, and average cost of service.

framework: Understand current competitive position: why patients are choosing UMC over Avicenna hospitals
Assess the viability of direct hospital competition with UMC (quality, brand, cost)
Identify non-hospital sites of care as an alternative channel to capture patients
Evaluate non-hospital site attractiveness using criteria: utilization, hospital replacement rate, capital intensity, revenue per service
Recommend short-term and long-term strategy based on analysis

questions.prompt: Why is direct head-to-head competition with UMC likely a losing strategy, and what alternative should Avicenna pursue?
questions.guidance: Candidates should recognize that UMC is described as 'one of the best hospital systems in the nation,' making direct quality competition difficult and capital intensive. Avicenna's unique advantage is that it is both a payer AND provider, so it can use insurance levers to steer patients to its own facilities or preferred non-hospital sites. The creative insight is to reduce the value of hospitals by driving members to non-hospital sites of care.

questions.prompt: Using the exhibit, which non-hospital site of care is most attractive for Avicenna to invest in?
questions.guidance: Candidates should evaluate each site against criteria such as revenue per service, hospital replacement rate, utilization level, and capital intensity. The key insight is that Infusion scores highest on revenue per service ($2,000) and is least capital intensive, even though its utilization is Very Low and hospital replacement rate is only 5%. Home Health has high utilization but low revenue ($500). Nurse Facilities have the highest replacement rate (80%) but moderate revenue and capital needs. Infusion is the recommended priority.

math.setup: Compare revenue per service and hospital replacement rate across the four sites to identify highest revenue with manageable capital requirements.
steps: Home Health: $500 avg cost, 60% replacement rate, High utilization
Hospice: $800 avg cost, 10% replacement rate, Low utilization
Infusion: $2,000 avg cost, 5% replacement rate, Very Low utilization — highest revenue per service
Nurse Facilities: $1,000 avg cost, 80% replacement rate, Medium utilization
Infusion has the highest average cost of service ($2,000) and is described as least capital intensive — making it the highest revenue-per-dollar-invested option
math.answer: Infusion is the most attractive site of care: highest revenue per service ($2,000) and least capital intensive, despite low utilization and replacement rate.

recommendation: (Good) Avicenna should avoid competing directly with UMC by leveraging its insurance position and building non-hospital services.

(Better) Avicenna should acquire high-quality infusion capabilities to drive customers away from UMC in the short and medium term, while reducing the role of hospitals across all services in the long term.
risks: Reducing hospital traffic at Avicenna's owned facilities may hurt short-term hospital profitability; may need to change or redefine the role of those hospitals.
Infusion represents lowest hospital replacement rate (5%), so the volume redirect is limited and must be supplemented with other non-hospital strategies.
Expect a competitive response from UMC; Avicenna must build long-term loyalty mechanisms to retain members.
next_steps: Evaluate acquisition targets or partnership opportunities in the infusion space in Chicagoland.
Model the financial impact of steering insurance members to non-hospital sites on both payer and provider P&L.
Develop a long-term member loyalty strategy to prevent UMC from recapturing redirected patients.
Assess regulatory and contractual constraints on using payer position to steer members.
